coverageNote: Disk enumeration matched the expected scope exactly: 8 units (the domain directory itself plus 7 sub-domain directories, each containing an *-index.md) and 45 .md files. Every file was read in full. Note that 03.07, 03.10 and 03.11 are flat feature files living directly in the domain directory and are therefore audited as part of the domain-root unit, together with community-networking-index.md, community-networking-cx.md and 03.09. Dimension 6 (Competitive Positioning) is N/A for all 8 units — it applies to meta/competitive-landscape.md, which is outside this domain. Dimensions 1-5, 7 and 8 were applied to every unit, giving 7 applicable checkpoints per unit and 56 in total. A large share of this domain is MoSCoW `Won't` (03.01.03, 03.02.03, 03.05.01/02, 03.07, 03.10, 03.11) or `Could` (03.05.03, all of 03.08); findings inside `Won't` units were held to the standard 'does this change what gets built' and dropped where the feature is explicitly retained for traceability only — several clean but inert contradictions in 03.01.03 and 03.07 were refuted on that basis during the devil's-advocate pass.

findings.claim: community-networking-cx.md CX-03 states both that scene membership IS a ranking axis and that it is candidacy and never rank. The two cannot both hold, neither carries a marker, and every other file in the tree takes the second position.
findings.evidence: community-networking-cx.md:128 (CX-03 detail) — "Step 6 hardened the coupling into a **one-way dependency** (03.06.01 DT-12): scene membership is a ranking axis, but a scene must never be *defined as* a feed weighting". Contradicted in the same file at line 14 (CX-03 map row) — "Scene membership is a **secondary fan-out set — candidacy, never rank**; ... The ranking axis is **geography** (03.02.02 D-03), an evidenced fact, not the join flag: per 03.06.01 D-08 ranking reads evidence, never membership" — and at line 138 — "the feed reads it as a **fan-out set only** — candidacy, never rank, per 03.06.01 D-08 and §4". Externally corroborated: 03.02.02-ranking-relevance-controls.md:84 — "**geography** is a primary ranking axis (DT-03, D-03); **scene membership is not one**. Per 03.06.01 D-08 ranking reads evidence, never membership, and membership appears nowhere in the input list above"; 03.06.01-scene-definition-membership.md:124 — "Membership is **not** a ranking input — per D-08 ranking reads evidence, never membership".
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the feed scorer carries a scene-membership term.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the feed scorer reads CX-03's detail paragraph — the domain-level cross-cut file, which is the authoritative synthesis artefact for inter-child coupling — and adds a scene-membership boost to the ranking function. A user who joins forty scenes now outranks a locally-credited musician in those scenes' feeds. This is precisely the failure 03.06.01 Q-07 was written to guard against ("the easy implementation of 'in your scene' ... is a scene-membership boost — which would smuggle a participation metric back onto the ranking axis and break domain D-03 quietly"), and it violates domain law D-03 (evidence beats participation) plus 03.06.01 D-08 ("Membership grants nothing"), which is the decision that licenses membership to be free, instant and unverified. A second implementer reading line 14 or line 138 of the same file builds no membership term at all, so the two produce different feeds from the same spec.

findings.claim: The domain-level Role Matrix assigns access levels that contradict the children's own Role Matrices and Role Lenses, and the explanatory note beneath it enumerates a set of Fan-Full features that is factually wrong.
findings.evidence: community-networking-index.md:77 — "| 03.01-connections-follows-endorsements | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | 👁️ Read-only |" versus 03.01-connections-follows-endorsements-index.md:41 — "| 03.01.01-follows | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | ✅ Full |" and 03.01.01-follows.md:31 (Fan Role Lens) — "Full | The **only** graph edge available to them". community-networking-index.md:82 — "| 03.06-scenes-communities | ... | 👁️ Read-only |" versus 03.06.01-scene-definition-membership.md:33 — "| Fan | Full (geo only) | Per D-03 they are members of **geo** scenes". community-networking-index.md:84 — "| 03.08-contests-challenges-beat-battles | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | ⚙️ Config | 👁️ Read-only |" versus 03.08-contests-challenges-beat-battles-index.md:44 — "| 03.08.01-contest-creation-briefs | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | ✅ Full | ❌ None |". The reading note at community-networking-index.md:96-97 asserts "the Fan's access is `Full` only where a feature was built for them (03.02 feed, 03.09 jams/open mics)", omitting 03.01.01 Follows — which the same file's Q-09 (line 131) calls out as "**03.01.01 Follows is a Must** — the edge the Fan's alert path rides on".
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a Fan may create a follow edge, join a geo scene, or an Operator may author a contest brief.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer scoping the Fan surface from the domain index — the pipeline key artefact downstream stages read first — grants the Fan read-only access to 03.01, so the Fan cannot press Follow. Following is the single mechanism carrying the Fan's whole stated success criterion (03.01.01:31, "never misses a show by an artist they follow") and is the domain's only `Must`. The matrix legend's "Access icons are shorthand" caveat does not rescue this: Read-only versus Full is an inversion, not a granularity loss, and the prose reading note makes a positive, checkable claim about where Fan is Full that the tree falsifies in three places.

findings.claim: The sub-domain CX file records auto-follow-on-connection-accept as an open possibility, while 03.01.01 D-12 records it as a ratified prohibition. The CX file was flagged for reconciliation and never reconciled.
findings.evidence: 03.01-connections-follows-endorsements-cx.md:58 (CX-02 synthesis note 2) — "**Trigger chain**: Accepting a connection MAY auto-create a mutual follow — a convenience most networks implement. If it does, unfollowing later must not silently sever the connection. `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`." Contradicted by 03.01.01-follows.md:180 — "| D-12 | **No auto-follow on connection accept** | DT-11. Credit-seeded connections (03.01.02 DT-03) would manufacture follows at scale and inflate the one number DT-06 shows is currency." 03.01.01-follows.md:145 (DT-11) explicitly flags the reconciliation that never happened — "This resolves `#CX-02` note 2 from this side — flagged for Step 6 synthesis, since the CX file is not this feature's to edit" — and 03.01.01-follows.md:152 repeats "**Step 6 must reconcile the CX file**". The domain CX independently ratifies the prohibition at community-networking-cx.md:118 ("a connection *accept* must **not** auto-create a follow") and community-networking-cx.md:387 (R-07).
findings.forcedInvention: Whether accepting a connection creates a follow edge.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer working the 03.01 sub-domain reads its own CX file, sees auto-follow described as the convention most networks implement with only an unowned `[PENDING]` against it, and wires connection-accept to create a mutual follow. Because 03.01.02 DT-03 pre-seeds connections from every verified credit, this manufactures follow edges at credit volume on day one. 03.01.01 DT-06 establishes that a follower count is booking currency consumed by domain 17, so the platform mints inflated audience numbers into a live commercial negotiation — the exact outcome D-12 exists to prevent. The two documents also disagree about whether the question is even open, so an implementer cannot tell whether to build it, defer it, or refuse it.

findings.claim: The expiry period for unanswered connection requests is marked with a bare `[PENDING]` carrying neither an owner nor a deferral target, even though the Behavior section makes expiry one of three load-bearing parts of the throttle mechanism and declares that mechanism settled.
findings.evidence: 03.01.02-professional-connections.md:48-50 (Behavior, layer 3 of three) — "**Rate limit** — outbound requests are capped per requester per rolling period, and unanswered inbound requests **expire** rather than accumulating an unbounded pending queue." 03.01.02-professional-connections.md:71 (Edge Cases) — "| Request is ignored indefinitely | ... | Requests expire — `[PENDING]` on the period. Expiry is preferable to an unbounded queue the Producer will simply stop opening |". No owner, no deferral stage. The file's own Q-01 covers only the cap's shape, and states the rest is settled: line 52-55 — "What the **default** protects against is settled; what remains an owner decision is the *shape* of the cap". Compare the same file's well-formed marker two rows down, line 77 — "`[PENDING — Step 5 Must-depth or /write-be-spec]` on the exact cooldown", and the sibling feature 03.01.01-follows.md:177 (D-09), which fixes exact numbers at this layer ("60/rolling hour and 500/rolling 24h").
findings.failure_scenario: DT-05 in the same file establishes that the quota alone is defeated without expiry ("the mechanism therefore needs three cooperating parts — a quota, a same-pair re-send cooldown, and inbound expiry — not one"), so the horizon is not optional. With no value and no owner, one implementer sets 7 days and a Producer's queue drains before they read it; another sets 90 days and the guilt backlog the mechanism exists to prevent accumulates anyway. Because the marker names no stage, the gap is invisible to every downstream gate — nothing in /create-prd, /write-be-spec or /plan-phase is pointed at it.

findings.claim: The primary query axis "in the room / remote OK" attaches the D-15 network-latency ceiling to the physically-co-located option and removes all distance constraint from the remote option — the inverse of how the ceiling works, and the inverse of how the sibling feature states it.
findings.evidence: 03.03.01-collaborator-search-browse.md:38-42 — "**Collaboration mode — \"in the room\" vs \"remote OK\" (primary axis, D-04, not a filter).** ... \"In the room\" hard-bounds distance to the D-15 playable radius (~a few hundred miles under the 25–30 ms desync ceiling); \"remote OK\" removes distance as a constraint entirely." The sibling supply-side feature states it the other way round: 03.03.03-open-to-status-availability-signals.md:37-38 — "**Scope** — the qualifiers ... remote or in-the-room (per D-15 a physics question, not a preference — the ~25–30 ms desync ceiling caps a playable radius)". The underlying finding, 03.03.01 DT-03 (line 109), is stated in terms of real-time versus asynchronous, not co-located versus remote — "per D-15 the ~25–30 ms desync ceiling makes real-time collaboration physically impossible beyond a few hundred miles — so distance is a *hard constraint* for real-time work and nearly irrelevant for asynchronous work". The radius itself is given only as "~a few hundred miles".
findings.forcedInvention: What "remote OK" means with respect to the latency ceiling, and the numeric radius bounding "in the room".
findings.failure_scenario: The platform sells remote real-time jamming (domain 08, whose retained justification per parent D-04 is precisely latency-aware matching). An implementer takes 03.03.01 literally: a searcher selecting "remote OK" who wants remote real-time play gets distance removed as a constraint entirely and is matched with someone 3,000 miles away, with whom real-time play is physically impossible — the exact outcome D-04 ("A matcher ignoring physics proposes collaborations that cannot happen") exists to prevent. A second implementer reads 03.03.03 and bounds the remote branch instead, leaving "in the room" as a driving-distance radius they must invent, since "~a few hundred miles" is the only figure given and is not a testable value.

findings.claim: 03.03.01 treats the open-to appetite signal as a query axis that constrains the candidate set and can be "relaxed", while the sub-domain CX explicitly rejects open-to status as a search filter and routes it through scoring only.
findings.evidence: 03.03.01-collaborator-search-browse.md:36 — "**The query surface** is built around one primary decision and four refining axes", listing at line 49-50 "**Appetite** — the open-to signal (03.03.03): what the person wants to do next"; line 73 (Happy Path step 3) — "System resolves candidates from the credit graph **and open-to signals**, filtering out blocked and unreachable people before ranking"; line 84 (thin-scene edge case) — "Widen radius / **relax appetite**". Contradicted by 03.03-collaborator-discovery-matchmaking-cx.md:108 (R-02) — "Considered open-to status as a *search filter* rather than a scoring input. **Rejected**: as a hard filter it is worse than useless, because the signal is unreliable and decaying (CX-01). Filtering on a stale boolean silently hides the right person; scoring on it with decay-awareness degrades gracefully. The interaction is real but flows through 03.03.02 (CX-01 + CX-03), not directly."
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a candidate lacking a matching (or any) open-to signal is excluded from results or merely ranked lower.
findings.failure_scenario: 03.03.03 D-02 makes signals opt-in and silent by default, so most of the population carries no appetite signal at all. An implementer following 03.03.01 resolves candidates from open-to signals and excludes everyone without one — in a thin scene that is nearly everybody, and the searcher sees an empty result set for a city full of people who would have taken the work. That is precisely R-02's stated failure ("filtering on a stale boolean silently hides the right person"). An implementer following R-02 returns them ranked lower, and the "relax appetite" remedy in 03.03.01's empty state has no mechanism to act on. The two produce materially different result sets from the same query.

findings.claim: 03.04.01 D-03 records fail-closed-on-unknown as a ratified decision binding on 03.04.04 by name, while 03.04.04 records the identical question as an open, unresolved product decision in both its States table and its Open Questions.
findings.evidence: 03.04.01-collaboration-graph-path-finding.md:225 (D-03) — "Traversal failure degrades to **`unknown`**, never to `\"no path\"` ... **All consumers fail closed on `unknown`.**" and line 169 — "Consumers must fail closed on `unknown`: 03.04.02 must not broker on it, **03.04.04 must not decide reachability on it**". Contradicted by 03.04.04-reachability-inbound-policy.md:89 (States) — "| Error | Traversal failed | **Fail open or closed?** Failing closed silently drops legitimate contact; failing open lets the flood through on every degradation. **Unresolved — Q-04** |" and line 129 — "| Q-04 | On traversal failure, does the policy fail open or closed? Closed silently drops legitimate contact; open lets the flood through exactly when the system is already degraded. | Agent | `/create-prd-architecture` |". 03.04.01's own cross-cut note is itself ambivalent, at line 210 — "Reachability must fail closed on `unknown` (D-03), which **sharpens its own Q-04**" — asserting the decision and the openness of the same question in one sentence.
findings.forcedInvention: The reachability policy's behaviour when graph traversal fails.
findings.failure_scenario: This runs on every inbound contact attempt (03.04.04:53, "a **hot path on every inbound contact attempt**"), so the branch fires under exactly the degraded conditions where it matters most. An implementer following 03.04.01 D-03 fails closed and, during any graph outage, the entire platform silently becomes unreachable — every DM, connection request and call response dropped with no signal to the sender, since D-03 in 03.04.04 forbids explaining refusals. An implementer following 03.04.04 Q-04 treats it as undecided and either blocks the slice or fails open, which lets the inbound flood through at precisely the moment the wall — the mechanism 03.04.04 DT-01 says exists to keep the Producer persona on the platform at all — cannot evaluate. Neither implementer can tell from the tree whether the decision has been taken.

findings.claim: Reachability is gated on the collaboration graph becoming "dense", and neither the density metric nor its threshold is specified anywhere, nor tracked by any open question — despite the gate being declared a hard sequencing constraint with MoSCoW force.
findings.evidence: 03.04.04-reachability-inbound-policy.md:59-61 — "only which rung is the default remains open, and it is density-gated (D-04): **until the graph is dense**, the default must behave as **Open** regardless of the chosen level, because a graph-based wall on an empty graph refuses everyone (DT-03)". 03.04.04:119 (D-04) — "Reachability is **density-gated** — permissive until the graph is dense". 03.04.04:98 (DT-03) — "Reachability is a **density-gated feature**: permissive defaults until the graph is dense, then walls become meaningful. **This is a sequencing constraint that MoSCoW must respect, not a tuning detail.**" 03.04.04:74 (Edge Cases) — "reachability **cannot ship before the graph is dense**. This is a hard sequencing constraint with MoSCoW force". The file's four open questions cover the default rung (Q-01), the domain-05 listing conflict (Q-02), policy disclosure (Q-03) and fail-open/closed (Q-04) — none asks what density is or where the threshold sits. The sibling that owns density measurement leaves the metric itself open: 03.06.02-scene-graph-density-map.md:99 (Q-02) — "What is the density metric — edges, components, path length, clustering?"
findings.forcedInvention: The density metric, its threshold, and its scope (global, per-scene, or per-user) that flips reachability from permissive to enforcing.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer must ship the gate to ship the feature and has no value to ship it with. Choosing too low a threshold turns the wall on early and reproduces exactly the failure DT-03 names — "Shipping this early makes the platform a ghost town by construction — and worse, it would look like the product working as designed" — because on a sparse graph nobody is within 2 hops of anyone and every inbound contact is refused. Choosing too high leaves the Producer persona unwalled and inbound-flooded, which DT-01 identifies as the failure that has killed every prior music-networking product. Two implementers pick different metrics and thresholds and the platform's contact model differs entirely between them, with no tracked question routing the decision to any stage.

findings.claim: 03.04.02 prescribes decay as the remedy for stale intro paths and cites a question ID that no longer holds that content, while 03.04.01 D-11/DT-14 reject decay outright and specify disclosure instead.
findings.evidence: 03.04.02-warm-intro-requests-brokering.md:64 (Edge Cases) — "| Path is stale — one session in 2009 | The broker barely remembers the target; the intro is a cold ask wearing a warm costume | **Decay (Q-03 on 03.04.01)**. Stale paths burn brokers faster than anything else |". Contradicted by 03.04.01-collaboration-graph-path-finding.md:233 (D-11) — "**Edges never decay and are never deleted.** Age is disclosed, never weighted | DT-14 — resolves parent Q-03/this file's Q-03 ... a decay weight is the system asserting what a human remembers with no evidence for it (domain D-04). Disclosure gives the requester everything the curve was guessing at." and 03.04.01:198 (DT-14) — "❌ REJECTED **as weighting** / ✅ CONFIRMED **as disclosure**". The cited anchor is also stale: 03.04.01's current Q-03 (line 250) is "Is graph integrity monitoring built at derivation time, or handled reactively by domain 24?", which has nothing to do with decay.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether stale paths are down-weighted or merely age-labelled.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the intro broker-selection list follows 03.04.02's own edge-case table and applies a recency decay to path ordering. 03.04.01 DT-14 identifies exactly why this is wrong for this domain — "Four records together, last one in 2009, means that person is in your life" — so the decay silently demotes the strongest available broker relationships. It also breaks 03.04.01 D-12, which requires paths to be ordered by (source class → shared-event count → recency) and "never a blended score". Following the cross-reference for guidance lands the implementer on an unrelated question about sybil detection, so the pointer supplies no correction.

findings.claim: D-11 states categorically that edges are never deleted, while three separate specifications in the same file require edge or node removal.
findings.evidence: 03.04.01-collaboration-graph-path-finding.md:233 (D-11) — "**Edges never decay and are never deleted.**" and line 80 — "**Edges never decay and are never deleted** (D-11). The fact is permanent — deleting evidenced history is the reconstruction failure run in reverse." Contradicted three times in the same file's Edge Cases: line 147 — "| **Dispute resolved against the claimant** | The fact was never true | **Edge removed permanently.** Any intro in flight that cited it fails closed |"; line 97 (via the sibling feature's parallel rule) and line 162 — "| **GDPR erasure** ... | Erasure must remove the human from the graph immediately | Node and edges non-traversable at once |"; and line 97 of 03.01.01-follows.md for the analogous suspension case — "Permanent removal deletes the edges".
findings.forcedInvention: Whether dispute-lost and erasure remove edges or merely suspend traversal.
findings.failure_scenario: Taken literally the decision is unsatisfiable: an implementer cannot both never delete an edge and remove it permanently when a dispute resolves against the claimant. A cautious implementer follows D-11's categorical wording and implements dispute-lost and GDPR erasure as soft suspension retaining the row. That is defensible for the dispute case but not for erasure, where retaining the edge alongside its evidence is retaining the personal data the erasure request removed — and the file itself notes the graph "must be able to drop a node without waiting" on domain 02/09. D-11's rationale is written entirely about decay and historical fact, so the over-broad "never deleted" clause reads as a general rule when only the decay half is meant.

findings.claim: The sub-domain CX asserts that the first person to claim a seeded scene becomes its steward, contradicting the same file's own permission rule, D-14, 03.06.01 DT-10, and the parent index which records this route as foreclosed.
findings.evidence: 03.06-scenes-communities-cx.md:84-87 (CX-04) — "claiming is one candidate answer to \"who steward-appoints\" (parent Q-04): **the first credible local to claim the seeded scene becomes its steward**." Contradicted in the same file at line 41 (CX-01 synthesis note 3) — "Membership of a seeded scene must not imply any authority over the seed data. **Otherwise the first person to join Bristol owns Bristol.**" Contradicted by 03.06.04-scene-seeding-claiming-cold-start.md:226 (D-14) — "This feature **consumes** domain 16's claim verification" and its cross-cut note at line 199 — "**permission boundary**: claiming a *premises* is not claiming a *scene* (`#CX-04`). D-14 scopes claiming here to records, not to governance." And by 03.06.01-scene-definition-membership.md:171 — "Claiming confers authority over the **venue record only**. Scene authority is stewardship (03.06.03), which is density-gated and separately appointed". The parent index records the route as closed: 03.06-scenes-communities-index.md:76 (Q-04) — "Claiming was the candidate answer (`#CX-04`) and is **now foreclosed** — 03.06.04 D-14 scopes claiming to **records, not governance** — so no route remains". The foreclosed reading nonetheless survives in two further places: 03.06.03-scene-stewardship-moderation.md:46 — "claiming (03.06.04) is one candidate answer" — and 03.06.03:89 — "claiming is a candidate appointment route (`#CX-04`)".
findings.forcedInvention: Whether claiming a seeded record confers scene stewardship.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the claim flow reads CX-04 and 03.06.03's Behavior section, both of which name claiming as the steward-appointment route, and wires venue claiming to grant scene stewardship. The first Operator to claim a room in Bristol acquires governance over the Bristol scene — the outcome 03.06.01 DT-10 and CX-01 note 3 both single out as the thing that must be impossible "by construction rather than by policy", and which 03.06.03 DT-01 identifies as delegating a livelihood-affecting exclusion power to a commercially interested party. Three of the five documents an implementer would consult still assert the foreclosed route.

findings.claim: The steward's power set — which the file names as the feature's central question — is left unspecified behind a marker with no owner and a deferral target that names a pipeline stage the tree has already completed, and no Open Question in the file covers it.
findings.evidence: 03.06.03-scene-stewardship-moderation.md:32-33 (the entire Behavior section) — "`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — the steward's actual powers are unresolved and are the feature's central question. The plausible range, from weakest to strongest:" followed by a five-row risk table (curate featured content / welcome arrivals / correct definitions / remove content / remove people) with no indication which are in scope. The marker carries no owner. The named stage has run: siblings in the same unit are marked complete against it (03.06.01-scene-definition-membership.md:5 — "**Status**: [DEEP]"; 03.06.04-scene-seeding-claiming-cold-start.md:5 — "**Status**: [DEEP]"), and 03.08.03-judging-voting-anti-gaming.md:110 states plainly "`/ideate-discover` Step 5 has run". The file's four Open Questions cover who appoints (Q-01), whether Operators may steward (Q-02), fan-majority legitimacy (Q-03) and unpaid labour (Q-04) — none asks what a steward may do. Only one power is fixed, at line 99 (D-02) — "Stewards do not remove people from scenes".
findings.forcedInvention: Which of the five candidate steward powers exist.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer has one prohibition (no removing people) and four unadjudicated candidates spanning "low — taste, not authority" to "high — content moderation by an interested party". One builds curation and welcome only; another additionally grants content removal and boundary editing, handing an interested local party — frequently, per DT-02, a venue owner who buys from and sells to the people they govern — the power to remove a competitor's content from the city's scene surface. Because the marker names no owner and points at a completed stage, no downstream gate is watching for the gap, and 03.06.01's Behavior §2 already depends on the unresolved power ("Splits are proposed by stewards (03.06.03) and are subject to that feature's density gate").

findings.claim: Stewardship is density-gated with no threshold value, and the CX defers the threshold to a parent question that asks something else entirely.
findings.evidence: 03.06.03-scene-stewardship-moderation.md:100 (D-03) — "| D-03 | Stewardship is **density-gated** | `#CX-03` — a 30-person scene needs no governance; appointing one manufactures politics. |"; States table line 71-72 — "| Ungoverned | **Below density threshold** | No stewardship | Unclaimed | **Above threshold**, no steward | Scene runs on platform defaults; claimable |". The threshold is deferred in the CX to a question that does not ask it: 03.06-scenes-communities-cx.md:73-76 (CX-03) — "**Where the threshold sits**, and whether stewardship should activate automatically, is unresolved (**parent Q-04**)" — but parent Q-04 (03.06-scenes-communities-index.md:76) reads "[OWNER] Who steward-appoints? Self-appointment invites capture ... platform-appointment does not scale", a question about appointment, not about a threshold. The metric the threshold would be expressed in is itself open: 03.06.02-scene-graph-density-map.md:99 (Q-02) — "What is the density metric — edges, components, path length, clustering? Each says a different thing".
findings.forcedInvention: The density metric and threshold at which a scene transitions from Ungoverned to Unclaimed, and whether that transition is automatic.
findings.failure_scenario: The Ungoverned → Unclaimed transition is a specified state change with no trigger value, so it cannot be implemented as written. The two illustrative figures in the tree are 30 and 3,000, two orders of magnitude apart, and 03.06.02 Q-02 leaves open even what is being counted — edges, components, path length or clustering — so "a 30-person scene" and "below the density threshold" are not the same kind of quantity. One implementer gates on member headcount, which 03.06.02 D-02 forbids ("Density is measured in evidenced collaborations, never headcount"); another gates on evidenced edges, which in a seeded scene is zero forever per 03.06.02 DT-03, so stewardship never activates anywhere. No open question in the unit routes the threshold to a stage.

findings.claim: What happens when an entrant withdraws after judging starts, or a submission is disqualified after votes are cast, is left to a bare `[PENDING]` with no owner and no deferral target, and is named in the CX as an unanswered state-transition conflict — in a sub-domain that is in scope to build.
findings.evidence: 03.08.02-submissions-eligibility.md:57 (Edge Cases) — "| Entrant withdraws after judging starts | Judges have already spent time; other entrants may be affected | `[PENDING]` |" — no owner, no stage. Named but not answered in the cross-cut synthesis: 03.08-contests-challenges-beat-battles-cx.md:88 (CX-03 synthesis note 5) — "**State transition conflict**: A submission withdrawn during judging; a submission disqualified after votes are cast." — the note terminates there with no resolution, unlike the other four notes in the same block. Neither 03.08.02's three open questions (credit generation, professional exclusion, sample clearance) nor 03.08.03's four (blind judging, conflict threshold, public voting, silent-judge fallback) covers withdrawal. The sub-domain is built, not cut: 03.08-contests-challenges-beat-battles-index.md:72 (Q-02) — "**RESOLVED — yes, kept in scope, but at Could.** ... all four children in [moscow-ledger.md] § **COULD (201)**".
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a withdrawal during judging is permitted, whether it forfeits the entry's frozen rights terms, and what happens to a verdict that has already been partly reached.
findings.failure_scenario: 03.08.02 D-01 freezes eligibility and terms at submission and 03.08.04 D-05 reverts losing entries entirely, so withdrawal sits between two specified states with no rule joining them. One implementer lets an entrant withdraw and revert their rights mid-judging, which lets a likely loser pull their work after seeing the field and lets a likely winner pull it to escape the brief's licence — reopening the terms 03.08.01 D-03 froze precisely so they could not be renegotiated once the strongest entry was known. Another refuses withdrawal outright, trapping an entrant's work under a licence they wish to exit. Because the marker names no stage, the CX names the conflict without answering it, and no open question carries it, the gap reaches implementation unflagged.
